name: Dashain
significance: Nepal's grandest and longest Hindu festival (15 days), celebrating the supreme victory of Goddess Durga Bhavani over the buffalo demon Mahishasura (triumph of good over evil) and Lord Rama's vanquishing of Ravana. Symbolizes familial reunion, reconciliation, rejuvenation, and divine blessings.
rituals: Ghatasthapana: Sowing barley and maize seeds in holy sand to germinate sacred golden Jamara sprouts
Fulpati: Royal ceremonial procession carrying sacred foliage, sugar cane, and banana stalks from Gorkha Durbar to Hanuman Dhoka
Maha Ashtami: Solemn Kalaratri night-vigil and sacrifices dedicated to Goddess Kali
Maha Navami: Solemn opening of Taleju Bhawani Temple (open to public exclusively on this single day of the year); Vishwakarma vehicle and tool worship
Vijaya Dashami: Elders apply red rice-and-curd Tika and tuck golden Jamara above the ears of junior relatives while chanting Vedic benedictions
Kojagrat Purnima: Night-long vigil awaiting Goddess Lakshmi's blessing of prosperity
Erection of soaring bamboo swings (Rote Ping / Lingay Ping) in rural village hilltops and city commons
Kite flying with colorful Changi kites across the Kathmandu basin skies to signal the close of monsoon
key_highlights: Family reunions, red tika, bamboo swings, flying kites, feast of mutton and sel roti.

name: Tihar & Chhath
lunar_month: Kartik Krishna Trayodashi to Shukla Dwitiya (Tihar); Kartik Shukla Shashthi (Chhath)
significance: Tihar (Deepawali / Yamapanchak) is a 5-day festival of lights celebrating the cosmic relationship between humans, sacred animals, Yama (god of death), and Goddess Lakshmi (wealth & fertility). Chhath, following 4 days after, is the grand Mithila Vedic festival revering Surya (the Sun god) and Chhathi Maiya for cosmic health, long life, and ecological purity.
rituals: Day 1 - Kaag Tihar: Offering cooked rice to crows as divine emissaries of Lord Yama
Day 2 - Kukur Tihar: Honoring dogs with marigold garlands, vermillion tika, and feasts in gratitude for loyalty and spiritual protection

Day 3 - Gai Tihar & Lakshmi Puja: Morning veneration of holy cows; evening illumination of houses with clay diyo lamps, colorful Rangoli floor mandalas, and welcoming Goddess Lakshmi with Deusi-Bhailo singing troupes
Day 4 - Govardhan Puja & Mha Puja: Worship of cows and oxen; in Newar tradition, Mha Puja (worship of the inner divine self) marking the dawn of Nepal Sambat (Newar New Year)
Day 5 - Bhai Tika: Sisters bestow seven-colored Saptarangi Tika, Makhamali (Globe Amaranth) garlands, walnuts, and blessings of immortality to brothers, receiving gifts in return
Chhath Nahay-Khay & Kharna: Ritual purification bath and sacred kheer rice pudding offerings
Chhath Sanjhiya Arghya: Devotees stand waist-deep in holy ponds/rivers at sunset holding winnowing trays (Soop) filled with Thekua sweets, sugarcane, and bananas
Chhath Bhorwa Arghya: Morning arghya offered to the rising sun, ending a rigorous 36-hour waterless fast (Nirjala Vrata)
key_highlights: Diyo clay lamps, rangoli floor art, marigold garlands, deusi-bhailo songs, brother-sister bonds, sunset/sunrise river offerings.

name: Indra Jatra
lunar_month: Bhadra Shukla Dwadashi to Ashwin Krishna Chaturdashi
significance: Historical 8-day Newar harvest celebration in Kathmandu honoring Lord Indra (king of heaven and god of rainfall) to express gratitude for agricultural rains, remember departed ancestors, and display state authority and divine royal legitimacy.
rituals: Yosin Thanegu: Raising of the sacred 50-foot ceremonial pine pole (Indradhwoja) harvested from Nala forest at Hanuman Dhoka palace
Kumari Jatra: Grand procession of the living royal goddess Kumari in a massive golden three-roofed chariot, accompanied by guardian chariots of Lord Ganesh and Lord Bhairav through core city streets
Majipa Lakhey Dance: Fierce masked demon dance running wildly through cobblestone streets to protective music
Pulu Kishi Dance: Humorous and spirited dance of Indra's sacred white wicker elephant racing through narrow alleys seeking its lost master
Mahakali and Sawa Bhakku dances staged on ancient public stone platforms (Dabalis)
Display of Sweta Bhairav: Opening of the gilded lattice windows of the colossal Sweta Bhairav mask, pouring blessed rice beer (Ayla) through a pipe directly into worshippers' mouths
Dasa Avatara dance enactments depicting the ten incarnations of Lord Vishnu in front of Basantapur palace
Lowering of the Yosin pole and floating it down the sacred Bagmati River to conclude the festivities
key_highlights: Living Goddess Kumari chariot procession, Majipa Lakhey masked dances, wicker elephant Pulu Kishi, Sweta Bhairav pouring rice beer.

name: Bisket Jatra
lunar_month: Chaitra Masanta to Baisakh 5 (Solar Bikram Sambat New Year)
significance: Ancient 9-day solar New Year celebration of the historic city of Bhaktapur. Commemorates the mythic slaying of two deadly serpent spirits that emerged from the nostrils of an enchanted princess, liberating the kingdom from terror and inaugurating renewal.
rituals: Dyapva: Ritual installment of Bhairavnath and Bhadrakali idols into their towering multi-tiered timber chariot at Taumadhi Square
Chariot Tug-of-War: Massive tug-of-war pulling the chariot between Thane (upper) and Kwone (lower) municipal quarters of Bhaktapur
Yosin Thanegu: Raising of a 55-foot straight pine tree trunk (Yohsi) adorned with two banners symbolizing the slain serpents at Bhelukhel
Yosin Kwo-Thalegu: Dramatic felling of the pole on the eve of New Year day, welcoming the new solar cycle
Sindoor Jatra in Thimi: Devotees carrying 32 palanquins (Khats) of deities through town while showering each other with vibrant orange vermillion powder

Jibro Chhedne (Tongue Piercing) in Bode: A designated Newar volunteer pierces his tongue with a 10-inch consecrated iron spike dipped in mustard oil and parades through the town with a burning bamboo brazier to safeguard the community from epidemics
key_highlights: Towering chariot tug-of-war at Taumadhi, felling of 55ft pole, Sindoor Jatra in Thimi, ancient tongue-piercing ceremony in Bode.

name: Rato Machhindranath Jatra
nepali_name: रातो मत्स्येन्द्रनाथ जात्रा (बुंग द्यः / भोटो जात्रा)
lunar_month: Chaitra Shukla Pratipada to Jestha (Spans weeks to months)
significance: Nepal's longest, oldest, and most revered chariot festival (established in the 7th c. Licchavi era). Honors Avalokiteshvara / Bunga Dyah as the compassionate rainmaker, patron of agriculture, and guardian deity of the Kathmandu Valley.
rituals: Snan: Ritual ceremonial bathing of the red wooden idol of Bunga Dyah at Lagankhel pool
Chariot Construction: Assembling a colossal 60-foot conical chariot at Pulchowk, built entirely with wooden pegs and cane ropes without a single iron nail, topped with a juniper plume
Rath Yatra: Thousands of devotees hauling the mammoth chariot through ancient stone-paved streets of Patan in successive ritual stages
Minnath Chariot: Small companion chariot of Chakuwah Dyah (Minnath) trailing the main chariot
Nya-kye-gu: Ceremonial dropping of a sacred coconut from the chariot roof at Lagankhel, believed to bestow children upon whoever catches it

Bhoto Jatra: Grand festival climax at Jawalakhel, where government officials and the head priest display the legendary jewel-studded vest (Bhoto) to the four cardinal directions before the President of Nepal and Living Goddess Kumari
Final transfer of the deity either to Ta Bahal (Patan) or south to Bungamati village for its six-month winter residency
key_highlights: 60ft nail-less cane chariot, coconut drop at Lagankhel, sacred jewel-studded Bhoto display at Jawalakhel.

name: Buddha Jayanti
lunar_month: Baisakh Purnima (Full moon of Baisakh / 4th Tibetan Lunar Month)
significance: The thrice-blessed supreme holy festival of Buddhism, commemorating Siddhartha Gautama Buddha's Birth at Lumbini (623 BCE), his Supreme Enlightenment (Bodhi) at Bodh Gaya, and his Mahaparinirvana (passing into final peace) at Kushinagar on the exact same full moon date.
rituals: Dusk-to-dawn lighting of tens of thousands of golden butter lamps and oil diyos around stupas and sacred garden ponds
Mass circumambulations (Kora) around Boudhanath, Swayambhunath, and Maya Devi Temple with continuous chanting of 'Buddham Saranam Gacchami'
Monks from Theravada, Mahayana, and Vajrayana traditions gathering to chant the Tipitaka, Heart Sutra, and Karaniya Metta Sutta
Grand holy procession in Lumbini carrying the sacred silver and bronze Buddha image around the Kenzo Tange central canal
Bathing of infant Buddha statues (Abhisheka) with scented herbal water and flower blossoms
Hoisting new five-colored Buddhist flags and hanging lungta prayer flags across hills and rooftops
Strict vegetarianism, acts of compassionate charity (Dana), releasing captive birds, and feeding pilgrims
key_highlights: Tens of thousands of butter lamps, peaceful sutra chants, stupa koras, Lumbini relic processions, acts of dana.

name: Mani Rimdu
lunar_month: 10th Lunar Month of Tibetan Calendar (Post-harvest full moon)
significance: The principal 19-day trans-Himalayan Sherpa Buddhist monastic festival of the Nyingma tradition. Reenacts the legendary establishment of Buddhism in Tibet by 8th-century master Guru Padmasambhava (Guru Rinpoche), vanquishing hostile local demonic forces to inaugurate universal peace.
rituals: Creation of an elaborate multi-colored sand mandala depicting the palace of Lord Buddha Amitabha inside the assembly hall
Consecration of sacred medicinal herbal pills (Rilbu) through weeks of secret meditation and mantra recitations by celibate monks
Day 1 (Wong / Empowerment): The high Abbot (Rinpoche) grants public long-life blessings to hundreds of assembled Sherpa pilgrims
Day 2 (Chham / Sacred Masked Dance): Monks in silk brocade robes, bone ornaments, and fierce deity masks enact the triumph of wisdom over ignorance to the clash of cymbals and bass horns
Day 3 (Jinsak / Fire Homa Puja): Monks perform a sacrificial fire ceremony in the stone courtyard to consume negativity and heal the cosmos
Destruction of the sand mandala and casting the blessed sand into the sacred Dudh Koshi river to symbolize impermanence
Nighttime community Sherpa folk singing, syabru step dancing, and drinking butter tea and chang
key_highlights: Cham monastic masked dances, sand mandala consecration, high-altitude Sherpa culture under Ama Dablam and Everest.

name: Losar
lunar_month: Poush Shukla Pratipada (Tamu), Magh Shukla Pratipada (Sonam), Falgun Shukla Pratipada (Gyalpo)
typical_gregorian_window: December to March (Tamu: Dec/Jan, Sonam: Jan/Feb, Gyalpo: Feb/Mar)
significance: The joyous New Year festival of the high Himalayan, Tibetan, Sherpa, Tamang, and Gurung communities. Marks the transition of the seasonal animal zodiac, renewal of vitality, community harmony, and auspicious fortune.
primary_regions: Himalayan Districts (Solukhumbu, Mustang, Manang, Dolpo, Rasuwa)
rituals: Tamu Losar (Gurung community in Dec/Jan): Gathering in traditional Gurung attire, Ghatu and Kauda dances, community feasts
Sonam Losar (Tamang community in Jan/Feb): Selo dances to Damphu drums, visiting monasteries and elders
Gyalpo Losar (Sherpa & Tibetan community in Feb/Mar): Main high Himalayan celebration
Guthuk: Eating the sacred nine-ingredient soup on the 29th day of the 12th month, with dough balls containing symbolic ingredients revealing character
Tossing roasted barley flour (Tsampa) into the crisp mountain air with triumphant shouts of 'Ki Ki So So Lha Gyalo!'
Replacing faded prayer flags with vibrant new five-colored Lungta across rooftops, ridge lines, and monasteries
Preparing crisp fried Khapse pastries and serving warm butter tea, Chang (Tibetan barley beer), and Tibetan dumplings
Monastic lamas perform elaborate sacred masked dances (Cham) in monastery courtyards
key_highlights: Three Losar traditions (Tamu, Sonam, Gyalpo), Guthuk dough dumplings, tossing Tsampa, fresh prayer flags, Cham dances.

name: Maha Shivaratri
significance: 'The Great Night of Lord Shiva', celebrating the cosmic convergence of Shiva and Shakti, Shiva's cosmic dance of creation, preservation, and destruction (Tandava), and his emergence as the supreme infinite Jyotirlinga (Pillar of Cosmic Light).
rituals: Congregation of more than one million Hindu devotees and over 5,000 Sadhus (Naga Babas, Aghoris, Bairagis) at Pashupatinath from across Nepal and India
Pre-dawn holy purification ablutions in the Bagmati River and sacred mountain streams
All-night vigil (Jagaran) beside sacred Dhuni wood bonfires, reciting Shiva Sahasranama and chanting 'Om Namah Shivaya'
Continuous ceremonial bathing (Abhisheka) of the four-faced Pashupatinath Mukhalinga with cow milk, curd, honey, ghee, sugarcane juice, bael leaves (Bilva Patra), and dhaturo flowers
Ash-smeared Naga Babas performing yogic asanas and blessing pilgrims in the Mrigasthali forest and Ram Mandir courtyards
Ritual intake of holy prasad (bhang and cannabis smoke) by ascetics as an emblem of detachment from worldly ego
Grand evening Bagmati Maha Aarti with synchronized brass lamps, conch shells, and Vedic mantras
key_highlights: 1+ million pilgrims at Pashupatinath, Naga Sadhus from Himalayas, all-night Dhuni bonfires, holy bilva leaf offerings.

name: Holi
significance: The jubilant Hindu festival of colors and love, welcoming the renewal of spring and commemorating the miraculous salvation of prince Prahlada and the burning of the evil demoness Holika in fire, proving that pure devotion conquers all malevolence.
rituals: Erection of the ceremonial wooden pole (Chir) draped with colorful cloth flags at Hanuman Dhoka palace to inaugurate Holi week
Throwing and smearing fragrant colored herbal powders (Abir) in radiant shades of gulal red, saffron yellow, jade green, and azure blue
Playful water battles with water pistols (Pichkari) and water-filled balloons (Lola)
Open-air music concerts, traditional Dholak drumming, and communal street dancing in Basantapur and Lakeside
Enjoying traditional festive sweets such as Gujiya, Malpua, and chilled Bhang-infused Thandai milk beverages
Chir Dahan: Burning the ceremonial wooden pole at midnight to symbolize the destruction of evil demoness Holika
In the Terai (Madhesh), celebrations continue with grand traditional Chaitavar folk songs and Mithila hospitality the following day
key_highlights: Vibrant gulal colors, Pichkari water play, lively Basantapur street concerts, festive gujiya and thandai, Holika dahan.

name: Tiji Festival
significance: Centuries-old 3-day sacred Vajrayana Buddhist festival of the Sakya tradition celebrated within the medieval walled kingdom of Lo Manthang (Upper Mustang). Commemorates the victory of the Buddhist champion Dorje Jono over his demonic father who afflicted the desert kingdom with water shortages, disaster, and pestilence.
primary_regions: Upper Mustang (Trans-Himalayan Rain-Shadow Kingdom of Lo)
associated_places: Royal Palace Square of Lo Manthang
rituals: Solemn unfurling of a monumental three-story antique embroidered Thangka portraying Guru Padmasambhava against the fortress wall
Monks from Choedhe Gompa dressed in heavy handwoven silk brocade robes, coral and turquoise necklaces, and fierce animal deity masks perform the ancient 'Tsa Chham' dance
Reenactment of the cosmic battle between Dorje Jono and the demon of drought to the rhythmic booming of Tibetan Dungchen horns and drums
Presence of the Mustang Royal Family (Bista dynasty) presiding over ceremonial court rituals in traditional regalia
Day 2 (Nga Chham): Mystical sword and dagger dances purifying the earth of negative elemental influences
Day 3 (Rha Chham): Expulsion of evil spirits; the Tsowo (lead dancer) slays demonic effigies molded from Tsampa flour and hurls them beyond the fortified gates into the desert canyons
key_highlights: Historic walled capital of Lo Manthang, 3-story antique Thangka, sacred Tsa Chham masked dance, Mustang royal presence.

name: Gai Jatra
lunar_month: Bhadra Krishna Pratipada (Day following Janai Purnima)
significance: A uniquely profound Newar carnival of remembrance and satire initiated by King Pratap Malla in the 17th century to console his heartbroken queen after the death of their son, demonstrating that death is a shared universal sorrow. Sacred cows guide departed souls safely across the mythical river Vaitarni to the afterlife.
primary_regions: Newar settlements across Nepal (Kirtipur, Bandipur, Tansen, Pokhara)
rituals: Families that lost a loved one during the past year parade a decorated sacred cow (or a young child dressed as a cow with painted horns, headdress, and yellow silk) through the historical city pathways
Bystanders and shopkeepers offer fruit, beaten rice, coins, and sweets to the parading children in memory of the departed
Ghintang Ghisi Twak: Fast-paced, rhythmic two-stick communal circle dance performed by hundreds of youth in Bhaktapur
Sharp political satire, theatrical street comedies, costumed impersonations, and publication of irreverent satirical gazettes poking fun at politicians, corruption, and societal hypocrisy
Vibrant cross-dressing performances and pride parades by Nepal's LGBTQ+ community in Kathmandu, celebrated openly on this holiday of acceptance
key_highlights: Cow-disguised children, Ghintang Ghisi stick dance in Bhaktapur, biting political satire, comedy street theater.

name: Vivah Panchami
significance: The glorious spiritual festival commemorating the divine Vedic wedding of Lord Rama (prince of Ayodhya) and Goddess Sita (Janaki, daughter of King Janak of Mithila). Serves as an enduring cultural and religious bridge connecting Mithila and Awadh across Nepal and India.
rituals: Arrival of the grand bridal procession (Barat) from Ayodhya, India to Janakpur, greeted with flower showers and royal music
Matkor Ceremony: Women singing traditional Maithili folk songs while gathering sacred earth from the banks of holy ponds
Dhanush Yagya Reenactment: Staging Lord Rama's breaking of Shiva's celestial bow (Pinaka) at Rangbhoomi Maidan to win Sita's hand
Jaimala Ceremony: Rama and Sita idols exchange consecrated flower garlands on an elevated stage under a shower of rose petals
Vedic Wedding at Vivah Mandap: Hindu wedding rituals performed with fire oblations (Havan) in the marble wedding pavilion according to ancient Mithila traditions
Tens of thousands of pilgrims taking holy dips in Ganga Sagar and lighting oil lamps along the illuminated ghats
Serving opulent traditional Mithila feasts featuring 56 bhog delicacies including Makhana kheer, Dal-Bhat-Tarkari, and sweets
key_highlights: Ayodhya-Janakpur wedding procession, Jaimala exchange, Vedic wedding rites at Vivah Mandap, Ganga Sagar illuminated ghats.
